questions.q: Which term designates a benign epithelial neoplasm arising from glandular epithelium or forming recognizable glandular patterns?
questions.explain: An adenoma is a benign epithelial tumour derived from glands or forming glandular structures (even if not derived from secretory glands, such as renal tubular adenoma). Adenocarcinoma is its malignant counterpart, whereas a papilloma forms finger-like projections on non-glandular surfaces.

open.q: Name the benign epithelial neoplasm derived from glandular tissue or forming glandular patterns.

questions.q: Which of the following tumours ends in the suffix '-oma' yet represents a highly malignant neoplasm rather than a benign tumour?
questions.explain: Despite carrying the '-oma' suffix typically reserved for benign mesenchymal tumours, melanoma, lymphoma, seminoma, mesothelioma, and hepatoma are malignant neoplasms.

open.q: Name a malignant neoplasm whose name misleadingly ends with the suffix '-oma'.

questions.q: Which neoplasm arises from totipotent germ cells and contains mature or immature tissues derived from more than one embryonic germ layer (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm)?
questions.explain: A teratoma originates from totipotent germ cells (most commonly in the ovary or testis) that differentiate along multiple germ cell layers, producing skin, hair, teeth, cartilage, respiratory epithelium, or neural tissue.

open.q: Name the germ cell neoplasm composed of recognizable tissues derived from more than one embryonic germ layer.

questions.q: How does a hamartoma differ fundamentally from a choristoma?
options: A hamartoma is a disorganized mass of tissues indigenous to the site, whereas a choristoma is microscopically normal tissue in an ectopic location
A hamartoma is a malignant sarcoma, whereas a choristoma is a benign carcinoma
A hamartoma arises exclusively in the ovary, whereas a choristoma arises exclusively in the brain
A hamartoma is caused by oncogenic viruses, whereas a choristoma is caused by ionizing radiation
questions.explain: A hamartoma is a benign malformation composed of disorganized mature cells native to the organ in which it occurs (e.g., pulmonary chondroid hamartoma), whereas a choristoma (heterotopia) is histologically normal tissue found at an abnormal anatomical site (e.g., pancreatic rest in the stomach).

open.q: What is the fundamental pathological difference between a hamartoma and a choristoma?
accept: Hamartoma consists of disorganized native tissue at its normal site while choristoma is normal tissue at an ectopic site
Indigenous disorganized tissue versus ectopic normal tissue

questions.sub: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.q: Which single pathological feature unequivocally distinguishes a malignant neoplasm from a benign neoplasm?
questions.explain: Metastasis—the spread of tumour cells to discontinuous secondary sites—is the most reliable hallmark of malignancy, as benign tumours never metastasize regardless of size or mitotic activity.

open.q: Name the single most reliable pathological hallmark that unequivocally proves a neoplasm is malignant.

questions.sub: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.q: Lack of cellular differentiation in a malignant neoplasm, characterized by marked pleomorphism, nuclear hyperchromasia, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and atypical mitoses, is termed what?
questions.explain: Anaplasia literally means 'to form backward' and denotes dedifferentiation or failure of neoplastic cells to resemble normal mature cells of their tissue of origin, a key cytologic hallmark of malignancy.

open.q: Name the lack of cellular differentiation in malignant tumours marked by pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, and bizarre mitotic figures.

questions.sub: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.q: Which term describes full-thickness cytologic and architectural atypia of a stratified squamous epithelium that has not yet breached the underlying epithelial basement membrane?
questions.explain: Carcinoma in situ represents severe pre-invasive dysplasia spanning the entire thickness of the epithelium from basal layer to surface while the basement membrane remains completely intact.

open.q: Name the pre-invasive neoplastic stage in which severe dysplastic changes involve the full thickness of an epithelium without breaching the basement membrane.

questions.sub: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.q: Which primary anatomical route of dissemination is most characteristic of carcinomas, whereas sarcomas more frequently spread via the haematogenous route?
questions.explain: Carcinomas preferentially invade local lymphatic vessels and metastasize first to regional draining lymph nodes (such as axillary nodes in breast cancer), whereas sarcomas characteristically invade thin-walled venules and metastasize haematogenously to the lungs and liver.

open.q: Which pathway of metastatic spread is most typical for carcinomas as opposed to sarcomas?

questions.sub: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.q: Why do venous metastases originating from primary gastrointestinal tract malignancies characteristically lodge first in the liver?
options: Gastrointestinal venous blood drains directly through the portal vein into hepatic sinusoids
Hepatocytes express high levels of epithelial cadherin receptors that trap carcinoma cells
The hepatic artery receives 80% of resting cardiac output
Lymphatics from the stomach empty directly into the caudate lobe of the liver
questions.explain: Venous blood from the stomach, small intestine, and colon enters the portal venous system, making the liver the first capillary bed encountered by haematogenously embolizing gastrointestinal tumour cells.

open.q: Why is the liver the most common site of haematogenous metastasis from colorectal and gastric carcinomas?
accept: Gastrointestinal venous blood drains via the portal vein to the liver

questions.sub: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.q: Dense collagenous stromal proliferation induced by invasive carcinoma cells—responsible for the hard, gritty consistency of breast scirrhous carcinoma—is termed what?
questions.explain: Desmoplasia is an abundant fibroblastic and collagenous stromal reaction stimulated by paracrine growth factors (such as TGF-beta and PDGF) secreted by infiltrating carcinoma cells.

open.q: Name the dense collagenous stromal reaction stimulated by invasive carcinoma cells that imparts a stony-hard consistency to tumours like breast carcinoma.

questions.q: Which malignancy is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women in Nigeria and across sub-Saharan Africa, strongly linked to persistent high-risk human papillomavirus infection?
questions.explain: Invasive carcinoma of the uterine cervix, driven primarily by high-risk HPV types 16 and 18, remains a leading cause of female cancer morbidity and mortality in Nigeria where organized Pap/HPV screening coverage is limited.

open.q: Name the gynaecological malignancy caused by persistent high-risk HPV infection that is a leading cause of cancer death among women in Nigeria.
accept: Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix

questions.q: Which non-neoplastic chronic inflammatory disorder predisposes patients to colorectal adenocarcinoma through persistent epithelial injury, reactive oxygen species generation, and regenerative hyperplasia?
questions.explain: Chronic inflammatory conditions—including ulcerative colitis, Barrett oesophagus, chronic atrophic gastritis, and chronic viral hepatitis—promote genomic instability and cancer development via sustained inflammatory cytokines and compensatory cell proliferation.

open.q: Name the chronic idiopathic inflammatory bowel disease that confers a markedly increased risk of developing colorectal adenocarcinoma after 8 to 10 years.

questions.q: Which proto-oncogene is the single most frequently mutated oncogene across all human cancers, encoding a monomeric membrane-associated GTP-binding protein that becomes locked in its active GTP-bound state by point mutations?
questions.explain: Point mutations in KRAS, NRAS, or HRAS (typically at codons 12, 13, or 61) abolish intrinsic GTPase activity and prevent GAP-mediated inactivation, keeping RAS constitutively bound to GTP and continuously stimulating the MAPK and PI3K growth pathways.

open.q: Name the most commonly mutated proto-oncogene family in human cancers, encoding a small GTP-binding signal-transducing protein.

questions.q: In chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), a reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11) creates the Philadelphia chromosome and fuses which two genes to encode a constitutively active tyrosine kinase?
questions.explain: The t(9;22) translocation juxtaposes the BCR gene on chromosome 22 with the ABL1 tyrosine kinase gene on chromosome 9, creating the BCR-ABL1 fusion oncoprotein targeted by imatinib.

open.q: Which two genes are fused by the Philadelphia chromosome translocation t(9;22) in chronic myeloid leukaemia?

questions.q: Burkitt lymphoma, an aggressive B-cell neoplasm endemic in equatorial Africa, is driven by a chromosomal translocation—most commonly t(8;14)—that places which transcription factor oncogene under the control of the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer?
questions.explain: Translocation t(8;14)(q24;q32) moves the MYC proto-oncogene on chromosome 8q24 adjacent to the constitutively active IGH locus on chromosome 14q32, driving rapid B-cell proliferation.

open.q: Name the nuclear transcription factor proto-oncogene on chromosome 8q24 activated by t(8;14) translocation in Burkitt lymphoma.

questions.q: In approximately 20% of invasive breast carcinomas, amplification of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene on chromosome 17q12 drives tumour proliferation through overexpression of which class of oncoprotein?
questions.explain: ERBB2 (HER2/neu) encodes an epidermal growth factor receptor-family transmembrane tyrosine kinase; gene amplification leads to constitutive dimerization and mitogenic signaling targeted by trastuzumab.

open.q: What functional class of oncoprotein is encoded by the ERBB2 (HER2) gene amplified in a subset of invasive breast carcinomas?

questions.sub: Molecular Basis of Cancer: Tumour Suppressor Genes
questions.q: According to Knudson's two-hit hypothesis formulated from studies of retinoblastoma, how many mutant alleles of a classic tumour suppressor gene must be inactivated within a single cell to initiate tumorigenesis?
options: At least four alleles in adjacent stromal cells
questions.explain: Tumour suppressor genes generally act recessively at the cellular level: in familial retinoblastoma, one defective RB1 allele is inherited in the germline ('first hit') and a somatic mutation inactivates the remaining normal allele ('second hit').

open.q: According to Knudson's two-hit hypothesis, how many alleles of a classic tumour suppressor gene must be lost or inactivated in a cell to cause loss of growth suppression?

questions.sub: Molecular Basis of Cancer: Tumour Suppressor Genes
questions.q: In its hypophosphorylated active state, the retinoblastoma protein (pRB) halts cell cycle progression at the G1/S restriction point by binding and sequestering which family of transcription factors?
questions.explain: Hypophosphorylated pRB binds E2F transcription factors and recruits histone deacetylases to silence S-phase genes; phosphorylation of pRB by cyclin D-CDK4/6 complexes releases E2F to drive DNA synthesis.

open.q: Name the transcription factor family bound and inhibited by hypophosphorylated retinoblastoma protein (pRB) at the G1/S cell cycle checkpoint.

questions.sub: Molecular Basis of Cancer: Tumour Suppressor Genes
questions.q: When cellular DNA damage activates the TP53 tumour suppressor protein ('guardian of the genome'), p53 induces transcription of which cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor to arrest the cell cycle in G1?
questions.explain: Stabilized p53 acts as a transcription factor that upregulates CDKN1A (encoding p21), which inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes to enforce G1 arrest for DNA repair, and upregulates BAX/PUMA to trigger apoptosis if damage is irreparable.

open.q: Name the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor transcriptionally induced by p53 to enforce G1 cell cycle arrest after DNA damage.

questions.sub: Molecular Basis of Cancer: Tumour Suppressor Genes
questions.q: Germline loss-of-function mutations in the APC tumour suppressor gene cause familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) by preventing the cytoplasmic degradation of which Wnt-pathway transcriptional co-activator?
questions.explain: Normal APC forms a destruction complex with axin and GSK3-beta that ubiquitinates beta-catenin for proteasomal degradation; loss of APC allows beta-catenin to accumulate and translocate into the nucleus to activate MYC and cyclin D1.

open.q: Name the Wnt signaling protein that accumulates in the nucleus and drives colonic epithelial proliferation when the APC tumour suppressor gene is mutated.

questions.q: In follicular lymphoma, the t(14;18)(q32;q21) chromosomal translocation causes constitutive overexpression of BCL-2, conferring which key hallmark of cancer?
options: Resistance to apoptosis (evasion of cell death)
Autocrine secretion of epidermal growth factor
Loss of contact inhibition via E-cadherin mutation
questions.explain: Overexpression of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 prevents mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and cytochrome c release, allowing follicular B lymphocytes to survive indefinitely without normal antigen-driven apoptosis.

open.q: Which hallmark of cancer is directly conferred by t(14;18)-mediated overexpression of BCL-2 in follicular lymphoma?

questions.q: Which metabolic adaptation, known as the Warburg effect, enables rapidly proliferating cancer cells to generate biosynthetic intermediates for nucleotide, amino acid, and lipid synthesis?
options: Aerobic glycolysis (high glucose uptake and lactate fermentation even in the presence of abundant oxygen)
Exclusive reliance on mitochondrial beta-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids
Complete suppression of the pentose phosphate pathway
Inhibition of all cell-surface GLUT glucose transporters
questions.explain: Cancer cells shift metabolism toward aerobic glycolysis (the Warburg effect), consuming large amounts of glucose and converting pyruvate to lactate despite adequate oxygen, thereby diverting glycolytic intermediates into anabolic biomass pathways.

open.q: What is the Warburg effect in cancer cell metabolism?
accept: Preferential glycolysis and lactate production even in the presence of oxygen

questions.q: During the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) required for carcinoma invasion and metastasis, downregulation of which calcium-dependent intercellular adhesion molecule detaches epithelial tumour cells from one another?
questions.explain: E-cadherin forms adherens junctions that maintain epithelial polarity and cohesion; transcriptional repression (by SNAIL and TWIST) or mutation of CDH1 (E-cadherin) loosens cell-cell contacts and promotes invasion.

open.q: Name the epithelial cell-cell adhesion glycoprotein whose loss or downregulation allows carcinoma cells to dissociate during invasion and metastasis.

questions.q: Which family of zinc-dependent extracellular endopeptidases—secreted by tumour cells and tumour-associated stromal cells—degrades type IV collagen in basement membranes and interstitial matrix during local invasion?
questions.explain: Matrix metalloproteinases such as MMP-2 and MMP-9 (type IV collagenases) cleave basement membrane collagen and release matrix-bound angiogenic growth factors like VEGF to enable invasive spread.

open.q: Name the family of zinc-dependent proteolytic enzymes that degrade basement membrane type IV collagen and extracellular matrix during tumour invasion.

questions.sub: DNA Repair and Cancer Predisposition Syndromes
questions.q: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) is caused by inherited germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes (such as MLH1 and MSH2), producing which characteristic molecular signature in tumour DNA?
questions.explain: Defective mismatch repair fails to correct strand-slippage errors during replication of short tandem repeats (microsatellites), causing widespread expansions or contractions in repeat length known as microsatellite instability.

open.q: Name the characteristic genomic signature detected in tumours from patients with Lynch syndrome due to defective DNA mismatch repair.

questions.sub: DNA Repair and Cancer Predisposition Syndromes
questions.q: Xeroderma pigmentosum confers a greater than 1000-fold increased risk of sun-induced skin cancers (basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma) due to an inherited defect in which DNA repair pathway?
questions.explain: Ultraviolet radiation induces bulky pyrimidine dimers in DNA that are normally excised by the nucleotide excision repair pathway; inherited NER deficiency leads to early childhood skin cancers on sun-exposed skin.

open.q: Which DNA repair pathway is defective in xeroderma pigmentosum, preventing repair of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers?

questions.q: In chemical carcinogenesis, how do tumour promoters (such as phorbol esters) differ from tumour initiators?
options: Promoters are non-mutagenic agents that stimulate clonal proliferation of already initiated mutated cells
Promoters cause irreversible direct covalent DNA adducts even when applied before an initiator
Promoters permanently repair DNA mutations induced by alkylating agents
Promoters induce malignant transformation without requiring any prior genetic mutation
questions.explain: Initiators are mutagens that cause permanent, heritable DNA damage ('first step'), whereas promoters do not directly mutate DNA and are non-tumorigenic alone, but induce clonal expansion of initiated cells when applied after initiation.

open.q: How do tumour promoters differ from chemical initiators in multistep chemical carcinogenesis?
accept: Promoters are non-mutagenic and induce proliferation of already initiated cells
Promoters do not directly damage DNA but drive clonal expansion after initiation

questions.q: A 46-year-old Nigerian farmer from a rural area with poor grain storage practices presents with a large right-lobe hepatocellular carcinoma. His tumour shows a signature codon 249 G-to-T transversion in the TP53 gene. Which fungal mycotoxin contaminated his staple crops?
questions.explain: Aflatoxin B1, produced by Aspergillus flavus growing on improperly stored grains and groundnuts, is metabolized by hepatic CYP450 into a reactive epoxide that binds guanine and induces a characteristic R249S (codon 249) TP53 mutation, synergizing with chronic hepatitis B infection.

open.q: Name the Aspergillus-derived mycotoxin that contaminates poorly stored grains and groundnuts and causes hepatocellular carcinoma with a signature codon 249 TP53 mutation.

questions.q: High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV types 16 and 18) drives cervical carcinogenesis primarily through the viral oncoproteins E6 and E7, which bind and inactivate which two host tumour suppressor proteins respectively?
questions.explain: High-risk HPV E6 binds p53 and targets it for ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation, while E7 binds hypophosphorylated pRB, releasing E2F and forcing unrestrained S-phase entry.

open.q: Which two host tumour suppressor proteins are inactivated by the high-risk HPV viral oncoproteins E6 and E7?

questions.q: Which oncogenic DNA virus infects B lymphocytes via the CD21 (CR2) complement receptor and is implicated in the pathogenesis of endemic Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and Hodgkin lymphoma?
questions.explain: Epstein-Barr virus (HHV-4) uses CD21 on B cells for entry and expresses latent viral proteins (such as LMP-1, which mimics constitutively active CD40) that drive polyclonal B-cell proliferation and predispose to MYC translocations.

open.q: Name the herpesvirus that enters B lymphocytes via CD21 and is strongly associated with endemic Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

questions.q: Chronic gastric infection with Helicobacter pylori predisposes not only to gastric adenocarcinoma but also to which low-grade B-cell lymphoma that can regress following antibiotic eradication therapy?
options: Primary central nervous system diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
questions.explain: Chronic H. pylori gastritis induces acquired lymphoid tissue in the stomach and polyclonal B-cell proliferation driven by H. pylori-reactive T cells; early monoclonal MALT lymphomas remain dependent on bacterial antigen stimulation and often regress after H. pylori eradication.

open.q: Name the extranodal gastric B-cell lymphoma induced by chronic Helicobacter pylori gastritis that often regresses after antibiotic eradication.

questions.sub: Clinical Aspects, Grading, Staging, and Paraneoplastic Syndromes
questions.q: In the TNM staging system for malignant solid tumours, what do the letters T, N, and M respectively represent?
options: Primary tumour size/local extent, regional lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis
Tumour grade, mitotic number, and necrosis percentage
Tissue origin, nuclear pleomorphism, and molecular markers
Treatment response, nodal biopsy date, and mortality risk
questions.explain: Staging (TNM) evaluates the anatomical extent of disease—T (size/depth of primary tumour), N (presence and extent of regional lymph node spread), and M (presence or absence of distant metastasis)—and correlates more strongly with prognosis than histologic grade.

open.q: State what each letter stands for in the TNM cancer staging system.
accept: Primary tumour size/extent, regional lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis

questions.sub: Clinical Aspects, Grading, Staging, and Paraneoplastic Syndromes
questions.q: How does tumour grading differ from tumour staging in oncology?
options: Grading assesses microscopic degree of differentiation and mitotic activity, whereas staging measures anatomical extent of spread
Grading is determined by CT scan, whereas staging is determined exclusively by serum tumour markers
Grading applies only to benign tumours, whereas staging applies only to leukaemias
Grading measures distant metastasis, whereas staging measures nuclear hyperchromasia
questions.explain: Grading (well, moderately, or poorly differentiated; Grades I–IV) is a histological assessment of how closely tumour cells resemble normal tissue of origin and their proliferative activity, whereas staging assesses clinical and pathological anatomical spread.

open.q: What is the fundamental distinction between histological grading and clinical/pathological staging of a malignant tumour?
accept: Grading evaluates microscopic cellular differentiation while staging evaluates anatomical extent of spread

questions.sub: Clinical Aspects, Grading, Staging, and Paraneoplastic Syndromes
questions.q: A 62-year-old heavy smoker with small cell lung carcinoma develops severe hyponatraemia (serum sodium 116 mmol/L), low serum osmolality, and inappropriately concentrated urine without peripheral oedema. Which paraneoplastic hormone is the tumour secreting?
questions.explain: Small cell lung carcinoma frequently secretes ectopic antidiuretic hormone (causing syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion, SIADH) or ACTH (causing Cushing syndrome), whereas squamous cell lung carcinoma typically secretes PTHrP causing hypercalcaemia.

open.q: Name the ectopic peptide hormone secreted by small cell lung carcinoma that causes paraneoplastic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIADH) and euvolaemic hyponatraemia.

questions.sub: Clinical Aspects, Grading, Staging, and Paraneoplastic Syndromes
questions.q: Which mediator is primarily responsible for paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia in patients with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, renal cell carcinoma, or breast cancer in the absence of skeletal metastases?
questions.explain: Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy is most commonly mediated by tumour secretion of PTHrP, which mimics parathyroid hormone by stimulating osteoclastic bone resorption and renal tubular calcium reabsorption.

open.q: Name the humoral mediator most frequently responsible for paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia of malignancy in squamous cell lung carcinoma.

questions.q: Why are serum tumour markers such as carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), CA-125, and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) unsuitable as standalone primary screening tests for cancer in asymptomatic populations?
options: They lack sufficient sensitivity for early small tumours and can be elevated in benign inflammatory conditions
They are detectable only in post-mortem tissue biopsies
They are completely absent in all metastatic adenocarcinomas
They require radioactive isotope injection into the patient prior to blood draw
questions.explain: Most serum tumour markers lack specificity (rising in benign conditions like cirrhosis, smoking, or endometriosis) and lack sensitivity for early-stage disease; their main clinical value lies in monitoring treatment response and detecting tumour recurrence.

open.q: What is the primary clinical utility of serum tumour markers such as CEA and CA-125, given that they lack specificity for population screening?
accept: Monitoring response to therapy and detecting recurrence
Monitoring treatment response and tumour relapse
